#6487. The Best Recipes to Bring to a Potluck, According to Eater Editors

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a big party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

Dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with big flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

#6486. Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

These red-wine-braised short ribs have fans. “This has been my go-to recipe for short ribs for as long as I can remember,” says one commenter. “It never fails.” It’s the kind of special-occasion dish you make once and return to forever.

Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings. A full bottle of dry red wine reduces by half before the broth goes in; a whole head of garlic and plenty of fresh herbs round out the braise. After that, a few hours in the oven turn the meat fall-off-the-bone tender.

Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them. Serve over mashed potatoes, soft polenta, or wide egg noodles to soak up every drop of the rich sauce.

Look for meaty, bone-in English-cut short ribs, with a single rib bone beneath each piece of meat. Ask your butcher to cut them crosswise into 2" lengths—you’re not expected to saw through the bones at home. Avoid the thin strips sold for grilling.

What’s the best wine for braised short ribs?

Choose a dry red wine you’d enjoy drinking. Cabernet Sauvignon is the recipe’s first choice, but Merlot or a Rhône-style red also fits the bill. There’s no need to splurge; save your special bottle for the table.

For the smooth sauce intended here, yes. The vegetables flavor the braising liquid, and straining removes them along with the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic skins.

For a more rustic approach, pluck out the herbs and garlic skins (leave the cloves behind) and use an immersion blender to purée the cooked vegetables into the sauce.

Start checking after 2 hours in the oven. A fork should slide into the meat easily, and a gentle twist should pull it apart. If the meat still resists, keep braising. The listed cooking time is a guide, not a hard stop.

Can I make these short ribs ahead, and how should I reheat them?

Yes. Finish cooking the ribs and strain the sauce, then refrigerate the ribs with their sauce in shallow containers within 2 hours of cooking. The next day, lift off the hardened fat. Transfer the ribs and sauce to an ovenproof pot or baking dish, cover, and reheat in a 350° oven until hot throughout—the meat should reach 165° in the center.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

Try this recipe with this expert pick from the Bon Appétit Wine Shop.

Staub Enameled Cast Iron Round Dutch Oven 7-Qt.

Preheat oven to 350°. Season 5 lb. bone-in beef short ribs, cut crosswise into 2" pieces by your butcher, with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Working in 2 batches, cook short ribs, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. drippings from pot.

Cook 3 medium onions, chopped, 3 medium carrots, peeled, chopped, and 2 celery stalks, chopped, in same pot over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onions are browned, about 5 minutes. Add 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until combined and deep red, 2–3 minutes.

Stir in one 750-ml bottle dry red wine (preferably Cabernet Sauvignon), then add short ribs along with any juices that have accumulated on the plate. Bring to a boil; reduce heat to medium and simmer until wine is reduced by half, about 25 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise, 10 sprigs parsley, 8 sprigs thyme, 4 sprigs oregano, 2 sprigs rosemary, and 2 fresh or dried bay leaves; stir in 4 cups low-sodium beef broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and transfer pot to oven. Braise until short ribs are tender, 2–2½ hours.

Uncover pot and transfer short ribs to a platter. Strain sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; spoon fat from surface and discard. Season sauce with salt and pepper. Arrange ribs in shallow bowls, over mashed potatoes if desired, and spoon sauce over.

#6485. Scientists Discover Two Monster Black Holes at the Dawn of Time That Shouldn’t Exist

A rare cosmic discovery offers new clues about how early galaxy interactions may have fueled the rapid growth of supermassive black holes.

Astronomers have discovered two enormous black holes shining as quasars just 900 million years after the Big Bang, challenging theories of how supermassive black holes formed in the early Universe. One contains roughly 1.5 billion times the Sun’s mass, while its companion weighs about 400 million solar masses.

The system, designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is the most distant compact quasar pair ever identified. Its two members are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way.

“There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” says Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab who led the international study. “We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”

Quasars are intensely luminous regions surrounding actively feeding supermassive black holes. As gas spirals inward, it heats up and releases tremendous amounts of radiation, sometimes outshining every star in the surrounding galaxy.

During the Universe’s first billion years, galaxies rapidly assembled within growing concentrations of dark matter. Galaxy collisions and mergers could funnel gas toward central black holes, fueling their growth. Yet the enormous masses of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remain difficult to explain within the limited time available.

The discovery emerged from the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) program led by Emanuele Paolo Farina of NSF NOIRLab/Gemini. Researchers examined 200 early quasars, representing approximately 43% of those known from this period, using Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit.

While inspecting the observations, scientists noticed that quasar J1602+4228A appeared to have a faint companion. Follow-up observations with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaiʻi confirmed that the two sources could be distinguished individually, despite their exceptionally close apparent separation.

“The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” says Onorato. Additional observations helped researchers further characterize both quasars.

Astronomers expect pairs of active black holes to form as galaxies interact and merge. However, black holes shine as quasars for relatively short periods, making it difficult to catch two neighboring objects in this luminous phase simultaneously.

The challenge is even greater in the distant Universe, where faint objects separated by tiny angles are difficult to resolve. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is only the third known quasar pair discovered during cosmic dawn, when the first generations of galaxies and black holes were taking shape.

Researchers suggest that Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua may lie in an exceptionally dense region of the early Universe, where frequent galaxy interactions supplied gas for rapid star formation and black hole growth. This remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed account of the system’s origins.

“Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” says Onorato. “It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”

The Hawaiian nickname translates to “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.” It was created through the A Hua He Inoa program in collaboration with Hawaiian language and astronomy institutions.

Reference: “Nāpōwawā‘enakaulua: A Close Quasar Pair at Cosmic Dawn in the Aether Survey” by Silvia Onorato, Emanuele Paolo Farina, Roberto Decarli, Klaudia Protušová, Elia Pizzati, Debora Pelliccia, Devin S. Chu, Larry Lindsey Kimura, Leinani Lozi, Emily Peavy, Fabrizio Arrigoni–Battaia, Eduardo Bañados, Aaron J. Barth, Silvia Belladitta, Manuela Bischetti, Sarah E. I. #6484. Galaxy Outflows Likely Regulate Star Formation At ‘Cosmic Noon’ NASA’s Webb Reveals

Sitting here on the outskirts of our Milky Way Galaxy, itâs hard to imagine the galactic machinations that led to our goldilocks spot around a very welcoming yellow dwarf star. But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation.

As observations by NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now reveal, massive galaxies have largescale gaseous outflows that greatly quench their star production.

And as the authors of a new paper in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science describe, JWST has observed a link between outflows from a massive galaxyâs central core and the quenching of star formation at so-called âCosmic Noon.â That is, roughly 8-12 billion years ago, when the number of stars forming per unit volume in the cosmos reached its peak.

Outflows are large-scale flows of gas, from inside to outside the galaxy usually caused by either supernovae or energetic outbursts from supermassive black holes.

These JWST observations have revealed that outflows are more abundant and more powerful than we thought, suggesting that the evolution of galaxies is strongly impacted by outflows, Sirio Belli, an associate professor at the University of Bologna, Italy and the paperâs co-author, told me via email.

Normally, galaxies are rich in gas, and when the gas is sufficiently cold, it collapses under its own weight and forms a dense cloud from which new stars form. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.

Growing supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies drive powerful winds, blowing away gas that would otherwise form stars, Rebecca Davies, the paperâs lead author and an astrophysicist at Australiaâs Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne, told me via email. With JWST, we can measure the amount of cold star-forming gas being ejected, Davies told me.

But JWST has also revealed that outflows powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes are linked to the rapid shut-down or âquenchingâ of star formation.

Quenching can happen if the galaxy runs out of gas or the galaxy stops being able to turn the gas into stars because the gas is too hot or turbulent to collapse, says Davies.

One possibility is that the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy releases a large amount of energy which removes and/or heats the gas and prevents the formation of new stars, says Belli.

As such massive galaxies age, their AGN become relatively quiescent, not unlike Sag A* --- our own Milky Wayâs supermassive black hole in our galactic center.

The Milky Wayâs black hole had a major flare just a few million years ago, smaller outbursts only a century or two ago, and it still flickers almost every day as hot gas swirls just outside it, says Davies.

A key open question is what triggers outflows powerful enough to quench galaxies.

Outflows are very common in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, but most of these galaxies are not quenching: the outflows simply keep the galaxies in equilibrium and prevent them from converting all their gas into stars too quickly, says Davies. Possible triggers of the most powerful outflows include galaxy mergers, or radio jets launched by the central supermassive black holes, she says.

As for how this stellar quenching might impact the formation of molecular clouds that spawn solar type stars and habitable planetary systems?

When galaxies are quenched, the formation of new stars and planets is shut down, with strong repercussions on the probability of developing habitable systems, says Belli. If the Milky Way had been quenched at Cosmic Noon, it would likely not have formed many new stars in the last 10 billion years, and our solar system which is only 5 billion years old would not exist today, he says.

But star formation can become too much of a good thing.

When star formation is too strong there are other problems, such as the large number of stellar explosions that could negatively impact the habitability of planets, says Belli. The connection between galaxy-scale processes and the habitability of planetary systems is only now being investigated, he says.

#6483. The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6481. China Signals Its Intention to Land on Jupiter's Moon Callisto

The China National Space Administration (CNSA) has been talking about a mission to the Jovian system since 2018. It's named Tianwen-4, and it will build on the success of other recent missions like Chang'e 6, which collected the first sample from the lunar far side in 2024.

Tianwen-4 obviously isn't a sample return mission. But according to recent developments, it will attempt another extremely challenging mission profile: a landing on Callisto.

The CNSA announced a new opportunity for payloads for its Tianwen-4 mission to Jupiter.

"The primary objectives of the Tianwen-4 mission are to achieve Jovian orbiting, as well as orbiting and landing exploration of Callisto, and to advance scientific research on the Jovian system," the announcement reads. To improve the mission's performance and success, the CNSA is asking for instrument proposals from within China and from outside partners.

The orbiter itself will carry 10 instruments, and the payload will include multiple cameras, imagers, and spectrometers, as well as a particle detector and a magnetometer. But the announcement also addresses the needs of a Callisto Lander.

"The lander is planned to carry 2 scientific payloads: Callisto Surface Composition Analyzer and Callisto Lander Magnetometer," it reads.

The surface composition analyzer will be a Raman spectrometer. Raman spectrometers can analyze the composition of rocks with the light from a laser, and are becoming a standard part of planetary missions. NASA's Perseverance rover uses an ultraviolet Raman spectrometer to measure fine-scale mineralogy and to detect organic matter. The ESA's upcoming Rosalind Franklin rover will have one, and JAXA's Martian Moons Explorer carries one in its IDEFIX rover.

Callisto's surface is heterogenous on a small scale. There are small bright patches that seem to be pure water ice and there are other patches that appear to be a mixture of rock and ice. These are intermixed with larger, darker areas that are not ice. But spectral identification is uncertain. The Tianwen-4 lander and its Raman spectrometer should be able to determine the compositions of these components. There's also lots of carbon on the surface, and the instrument should be able to tell if its primordial carbon or altered carbon.

This mosaic of Callisto images from the Voyager 1 mission shows a large-scale feature named Valhalla. It's an old impact crater with concentric rings expanding outward. They extend outward for about 1,500 km, and a bright central point, probably the original impact basin, is about 600 km across. Image Credit: NASA/JPL

While Jupiter's other moons like Ganymede, and especially Europa, have strong evidence for subsurface oceans, Callisto's composition and structure is less certain. It appears to be partially differentiated, and magnetometer readings are ambiguous regarding an ocean. But if the Tianwen-4 lander's Raman spectrometer can determine if some of its surface composition is aqueously altered, that would be evidence in favour of an ocean.

The lander's other instrument will be a surface magnetometer. By combining its data with the data from the orbiter's magnetometer, ionospheric signals and signals from the moon's surface can be separated. That will reveal more about its interior, especially regarding its potential subsurface ocean.

It would be nice to have a better understanding of Callisto, since it and the other Galilean moons are expected to have formed in-situ, unlike some other Solar System moons. Some of those appear to be captured objects. So understanding Callisto is an avenue to understanding Jupiter itself, the dominant planet in our system.

Callisto's internal structure is uncertain, but it seems to be differentiated, with multiple ice layers and a rock and metal core. It may also have a saltwater ocean, but is far from certain. Image Credit: By Kelvinsong - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31643955

Landing on any of the Galilean moons is challenging, but Callisto might be the least challenging. It's probably not the best scientific destination among them, but it is the most accessible. For one thing, it's outside Jupiter's extremely powerful radiation belts, where radiation is strong enough to degrade sensitive instruments after short exposure times. Think of NASA's Juno spacecraft and its wide orbit. It only makes short dives into the radiation belts. Even then, Juno protects its most sensitive parts inside a titanium vault.

Callisto is furthest from Jupiter compared to the other three Galilean moons, so its gravity well is shallower. Less precious propellant is required to land there. Tianwen-4 can also use gravity assists at Callisto to prepare for orbital insertion.

Callisto is further away from Jupiter than the other Galilean moons. The other three are deeper inside its magnetic fields and powerful radiation belts, which makes visiting them much more hazardous. The radiation dose on Callisto's surface is weaker and won't take such a heavy toll on sensitive electronics. Image Credit: By B. Smithin Szalay, J. R., Smith, H. T., Zirnstein, E. J., McComas, D. J., Begley, L. J., Bagenal, F., et al. (2022). Water-group pickup ions from Europa-genic neutrals orbiting Jupiter. Geophysical Research Letters, 49, e2022GL098111.

Another reason Callisto is the preferred moon for a surface mssion is the its surface. Callisto's surface is ancient, cratered, and stable. It's a geologically quiet place compared to Io, for instance. It doesn't suffer from the same tidal heating and constant volcanic upheaval that Io suffers from. There are no mountains or volcanoes, only ancient crater on top of ancient crater. This makes hazard avoidance easier, since orbital images are unlikely to have changed from the time they were captured to the time the lander arrives there.

But Callisto is still challenging. It's an airless moon, and that creates its own difficulties. Atmospheric breaking isn't an option. The time delay also ranges from about 35 to 50 minutes, so round-trip communication is double that. That means the landing must be autonomous.

The best surface images come from the Galileo mission, and that spacecraft imaged most of Callisto at poor resolution. Only some small areas are imaged at higher resolutions of tens of meters per pixel.

This image of Callisto is made from data from Galileo and Voyager 1 and 2. It emphasizes how heavily cratered the moon's ancient surface is, and how uniform it is. There are a few smooth areas, and no mountains of volcanoes. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/DLR

But the mission plan calls for Tianwen-4 to orbit Callisto at an altitude of 300 km. Galileo got to within 138 km of the moon, but that was 25 years ago. Camera technology has advanced since then, and Tianwen-4 will carry a pair of visible light imaging cameras. One of them, the wide-angle camera (JWAC), is dedicated to mapping Callisto's surface and topography. Tianwen-4's proposed mapping orbit is 300 km in altitude. From that height, the JWAC operates at about 90 meters per pixel.

In 2020, the CNSA outlined a timeline for the Tianwen-4 mission that would see it launch in September of 2029. To preserve precious propellant, the spacecraft will perform a slingshot flyby of Venus in April 2030, then a pair of slingshots with Earth in 2031 and 2033.

In 2035 it will reach Jupiter and enter an orbit around the gas giant, also making flybys of irregular moons. That's phase one. Phase two starts with two gravity assists with Callisto, then in February 2038, it will enter an orbit around the moon. At some point after that, the Callisto lander will be released.

This plan was first outlined in 2020, so it will likely be changed. The instrumentation on the orbiter could be changed, too, and that includes its mapping camera and its resolution. But with their call for instrument proposals, the CNSA is making one thing clear: they intend to land on Callisto.

#6480. Scientists Discover a Bizarre Quantum State That Exists at Room Temperature

With each laser pulse, a room-temperature supersolid selects a new arrangement, revealing how crystal-like order can emerge without being locked to one position.

Studying unusual quantum states often requires expensive equipment that cools samples almost to absolute zero. Researchers have now observed a supersolid at room temperature, using a system that strongly links light and matter. This unusual state combines the repeating pattern of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a superfluid.

A superfluid has no viscosity, the internal resistance that opposes flow in an ordinary fluid, so it can pass through extremely narrow channels without resistance. If you moved an oar through one, you would feel almost no drag until you exceeded a critical speed, when swirling quantum vortices would appear. A supersolid retains this fluid behavior while developing crystal-like order.

The TopoLight consortium’s study, published in Science Advances, involved researchers from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology in Poland, IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS).

The team built its system around an optical microcavity, a tiny structure that confines light. It contained a specially designed liquid crystal and a coating of organic semiconductor, a combination that allowed light and matter to interact strongly at room temperature. The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich, where researchers deposited thin semiconductor films onto photonic structures fabricated at the Military University of Technology.

“We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material,” says Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. “This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity.”

Inside the cavity, light and electronic excitations in the material become strongly coupled, behaving as hybrid entities called exciton polaritons. These quasiparticles last only a few picoseconds, with each picosecond equal to one trillionth of a second. Even that brief lifetime is enough for them to form a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which many particles share a quantum state and behave as a coordinated whole. Such a condensate can act as a quantum superfluid.

Building the sample also started a countdown. The organic semiconductor gradually reacted with the liquid crystal, leaving the researchers only a few hours after assembly to complete all their measurements.

“We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance,” recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper’s first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. “Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample.”

The transition to a supersolid showed up as regularly spaced bright fringes in the emitted light. These stripes revealed that the condensate’s density had spontaneously developed a repeating pattern, a hallmark of crystal-like order.

The stripes appeared in a different position with every laser pulse used to excite the sample. Each time, the system selected one of several equally possible arrangements, rather than reproducing a pattern fixed in place.

“This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking,” explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). “Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed.”

The emitted light also displayed a persistent spin helix, a repeating pattern in its polarization, which describes the orientation of the light’s oscillations. The condensate therefore showed two distinct forms of order at once, one in light intensity and another in polarization.

Physicists predicted supersolids as early as the 1960s, but experimental observations took more than half a century to arrive. In 2017, researchers observed supersolidity in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. The new work shows that similar quantum phenomena can be explored in photonic systems operating at room temperature.

“Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C,” says Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures. That is about 140°F.

The microcavities also provide the first electrically tunable platform for investigating supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. Applying an external voltage lets researchers dynamically change their optical properties, providing a flexible way to explore quantum phases of light and matter.

That control could help researchers develop practical quantum devices based on light. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, neuromorphic computing accelerators that take inspiration from the brain, and highly sensitive optical sensors that exploit the supersolid phase’s exceptional sensitivity to polarization.

Reference: “Observation of a supersolid phase in a spin-orbit coupled exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate” by Marcin Muszyński, Pavel Kokhanchik, Rafał Mirek, Darius Urbonas, Pietro Tassan, Piotr Kapuściński, Przemysław Oliwa, Ioannis Georgakilas, Thilo Stöferle, Rainer F. Mahrt, Michael Forster, Ullrich Scherf, Dmitriy Dovzhenko, Rafał Mazur, Przemysław Morawiak, Wiktor Piecek, Przemysław Kula, Barbara Piętka, Dmitry Solnyshkov, Guillaume Malpuech and Jacek Szczytko, 16 October 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee4875

#6479. The Absolute Best Pie Recipes, According to Eater Staff

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

#6478. 31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a big bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

Or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a big pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

Red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

These impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

For a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

If you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

This pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

Give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Plan for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

Cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

If your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

There’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a big crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

The stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

This dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

#6477. Did The First Quarks and Gluons Experience Brownian Motion? Sometimes.

There are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe. One is to peer into the deepest, darkest regions of space. The other is to study the most dense energetic fluid we can create in particle accelerators. A new study looks at how this fluid can behave.

The fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos. In those earliest moments quarks churned among the sea of strong-force carrier particles, similar to the way dust particles dance in a swirl of atomosphere molecules. Only after the Universe expanded a bit did this fluid solidify into the nuclei we see today. By slamming particles together at near light speeds, we can recreate a bit of that early plasma fluid, but only for the briefest moments of time. So we study the fluid primarily by the particles generated by these collisions. In this new study the team simulated how the fluid behaves when a heavy particle passes through it. In the lab this can be done by slamming a proton into a heavy nucleus.

Particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion. First observed by Robert Brown as the jiggly motion of pollen in water, it occurs when smaller particles collide with a larger particle over time. The barrage of kicks nudges the larger particle around a jiggly random path. The smaller particles also collide with each other in a similar way. On a large scale this creates many of the features of thermodynamics, such as the flow of heat and the ideal gas relation of temperature and pressure.

One of the features of Brownian motion is that the distribution of particle speeds is Gaussian. Most of the particles have speeds close to the average, but there are some particles that are much faster and some that are much slower. The distribution is symmetrical; for every 10 particles moving twice as fast as the average, there should be about 10 moving half as fast. This makes sense because collisions are random.

How the Gaussian particle distribution is shifted for higher-energy collisions. Credit: Du Plessis et al.

Although a dense plasma of charged gluons is very different from a drop of water molecules, they both follow this Gaussian distribution. After all, they are both a sea of randomly colliding molecules. You would expect then that when heavy particles move through the plasma, the result would be Gaussian. All the heavy particles would be slowed down passing through the plasma, but some would slow a bit more and others a bit less because of the random collisions. This new study found that for heavy quarks in a quark-gluon plasma this is only partially true.

At slower speeds the result is precisely what we would expect. Collisions are random, and heavy quarks would have a Gaussian speed distribution. But if the heavy quarks are moving at near-light speed, such as a proton in a particle collider, then the distribution is biased. The quark is much more likely to be kicked in a way that slows it down and much less likely to get a kick that speeds it up. This skews the distribution away from Gaussian.

This means that when we study quark-gluon plasmas in a particle accelerator, we must take this bias into account. Using this result, we can better understand the fluid as a whole, and this could help us understand the connection between the hot dense state of the Big Bang and the Universe we see today.

Du Plessis, Jean F., and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld. "Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm." Physical Review Letters 137.19 (2026): 192302. ↩

Brian Koberlein is an astrophysicist and author of the books Astrophysics Through Computation and Radio Sky: 40 Years of the Very Large Array. You can find more of his work on his website.

#6476. Quantum Breakthrough: Scientists Develop a Detector That Can Count Over 9,000 Photons

A new detector can measure hundreds of photons with less than a single photon’s uncertainty, offering scientists a sharper way to investigate quantum light and advance future technologies.

Scientists developing powerful quantum computers and highly sensitive cameras need ways to count individual particles of light, even when thousands arrive together. Researchers at Paderborn University in Germany have developed a detection system capable of counting from zero to more than 9,000 photons, opening new possibilities for studying quantum light and making precise optical measurements.

“Precisely counting photons becomes more challenging as their numbers increase,” said Timon Schapeler from Paderborn University. “Our approach extends photon counting to larger numbers of photons, bridging the gap between single-photon measurements and high-sensitivity optical power meters.”

Conventional detectors struggle with this task. Devices such as avalanche photodiodes typically register whether light is present without revealing how many photons arrived. Detectors designed for larger amounts of light face another problem because electrical noise makes individual photons difficult to distinguish. To overcome these limitations, the researchers combined superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), known for their efficiency, precise timing, and low noise, with a technique called multiplexing.

“We wanted to know how high we can push the number of photons that can be counted with SNSPDs,” said Schapeler. “This led to a detector system that uses multiplexing and the intrinsic photon-number resolution of SNSPDs. Although these technologies have been individually studied, there has not previously been a demonstration of using both approaches together at this scale, which is an order of magnitude larger than previous multiplexed single-photon counting systems.”

Previous research had shown that SNSPDs could distinguish limited numbers of photons using precise timing measurements. To expand that capability, the team divided a single light pulse into 128 smaller pulses separated in time, then distributed them across eight detectors to create 1,024 detection bins. This arrangement spreads the incoming photons across smaller measurements while retaining information about how many photons each bin receives.

“Our approach uses low-loss optical components to distribute light evenly across 1,024 detection bins while preserving photon-number information in each bin,” said Tim Bartley from Paderborn University. “This enables precise measurements, while multiplexing expands the range of photon numbers the system can measure.”

The researchers also used a detector model previously developed with Mariia Sidorova from PTB in Germany to characterize each detection bin and improve measurement accuracy. Testing laser pulses averaging between 1 and 15,000 photons, they demonstrated precise counts of up to 276 photons with uncertainty below a single photon. Achieving comparable precision with a conventional multiplexed system would require approximately 37,000 detector elements, compared with their 1,024 detection bins.

The findings, published in Optica, Optica Publishing Group’s journal for high-impact research, could help scientists develop larger quantum systems that use light to process information.

“Large-scale measurement of individual photons is a cornerstone of photonic quantum computing and single-photon-level imaging,” said Bartley. “With this new macroscopic photon-counting technology, we can learn a lot about how photonic quantum computers and single-photon-sensitive cameras can be scaled.”

Although the system has only been tested with laser pulses, the researchers plan to apply it to bright quantum states of light to investigate quantum effects at larger scales. Continued improvements in SNSPD technology could also support more precise and highly sensitive measurements across a range of sensing applications.

Reference: “Macroscopic photon counting beating the Poisson noise limit” by 19 November 2026, Optica. DOI: 10.1364/OPTICA.604389

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

WHY？WHY？WHY？“Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched;

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

Einstein’s sorrowful silhouette has faded into the distance. But his intuition, his persistence, his belief in “local realism”, has finally found its rightful home in the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT). Einstein was not a failed prophet, but a true physicist misunderstood by his era.

—— https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2088659998394077633

Within the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT), “quantum” should not be regarded as a fundamental ontological concept, but rather understood as the macroscopic manifestation of topological constraints, phase coherence, and defect stability within vortex networks. When superposition, entanglement, discrete spectra, and spin can all be geometrically explained via topological spin and topological defects, “quantum” retreats from being the ultimate explanation to merely a phenomenological label. If charge and spin can be interpreted through winding numbers or topological charges; if entanglement correlations can be explained by shared vortex structures; and if the probability amplitude squared law can be accounted for by geometric phase interference—then is there really any necessity for this imaginary “undead cat” of “quantum” to continue occupying an ontological position?

Scientists need to wake up and answer: You keep saying “quantum,” but can you actually define it without using circular logic? Is the world truly “quantum,” or is that just a label you paste over your ignorance? How many “quantum states” do you need to invent before you admit the model is broken? Is every observation a quantum state, or just a convenient fiction to fit your equations? Be honest: What is the real difference between “quantum mysticism” and divine revelation? If mathematical code predicts nothing but probability, how is it different from religious doctrine? The ultimate question: Is the universe built on tangible geometry, or is it just a ghost in your mathematical machine?

One of the most shameless experiments in the history of physics is particle collision; any result obtained through such destructive disassembly is absolutely not the original form of cosmic matter. Once they understand topological spin, the so-called scientists will naturally be able to tell right from wrong.

Entanglement is not a ghostly link between two particles, but the simultaneous manifestation of a continuous vortex whole at two locations. This aligns more closely with fluid mechanics, topology, and geometric intuition than with “quantum mysticism,” and fits better with the path of restoring physical reality to continuous media and topological structures.

detector over 9000, editor must have seen DBZ

If a self-organized material system in nature is artificially shattered, will it necessarily return to its original material state? If it can, that is typical particle-physics thinking. The term “quantum” is the baneful consequence of the lingering ghost of particle physics.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041
